claim: The canonical Go domain types and the command/event envelope types are implemented and verified. Exact decimal semantics, timestamp canonicalisation, the closed error taxonomy, and the aggregate/identifier agreement invariants all hold in Go. This is PARTIAL completion of WI-110: the JSON wire binding and the conformance corpus runner are NOT implemented, so binding_conformance.status_by_binding.go remains NOT_IMPLEMENTED and is NOT claimed as anything else.
method: Implemented decimal.go, money.go, error.go, envelope.go. Wrote 62 Go tests derived from the schemas and the shared corpus rather than from the implementation, so a change to the implementation cannot redefine what the contract accepts. Ran go build, go vet, go test -count=1, go test -race -count=1, and gofmt -l in contracts/go. Separately probed time.Parse against Go 1.26.2 to establish which inputs the standard library accepts, rather than assuming. Verified the float guard by introducing a deliberate violation and confirming the guard fails, then removing it.
result: All 62 new tests pass, plus 19 pre-existing identifier tests. go vet clean. gofmt -l empty. go test -race -count=1 clean. The float64/float32 guard scans 17 Go files across all six go.work modules and was confirmed to fail on an injected violation. money.schema.json minLength: there is none, so a single-digit amount is valid; a test asserting a 2-character minimum was corrected. decimal.schema.json supplies maxLength 40 and no minLength.
defect_found_and_fixed: (1) decimal.Sub computed d + o - o, silently returning the left operand. (2) Add and Sub had invalid return signatures and did not compile. (3) NewContractError initially returned a closure as an error value instead of a ContractError. (4) money.schema.json wraps a currency mismatch in the generic ErrInvalidMoney, so a caller could not errors.Is the specific invariant; added a distinct ErrCurrencyMismatch sentinel, since the schema names it as its own invariant. (5) Money had no Sub, Cmp, or Equal, so a ledger could not compute a difference, a comparison, or balance equality; all three added and currency-checked. (6) A test comment claimed time.Parse accepts a space separator; a direct probe showed it rejects that one while accepting a numeric offset and a tenth fractional digit, so the comment and the error.go rationale were corrected to match the measured behaviour. (7) Three test files were written against an assumed API (MustNewMoney, MustParseIdentifier, HasPrefix, a 2-character currency minimum, quantity sign rejection) that did not exist or contradicted the schemas; all were rewritten against the verified API and schemas. (8) Two tests tried to reach a rejection through a panicking Must* helper that rejected the input first, so they could never observe it; rewritten.
significance: Quantity sign is the subtlest finding: quantity.schema.json states that positive and negative quantities are both valid because direction is carried by the order side, not the sign. A binding that rejected negatives would force a short position to be recorded as a positive quantity plus a side, which is how a sell becomes a buy. Separately, command-envelope schema_version uses ^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$, which is looser than SemVer 2.0.0 because it permits leading zeros such as 01.0.0. The binding matches the schema rather than SemVer, since a binding stricter than the contract would reject documents the schema accepts and would break the agreement the corpus exists to detect. Tightening this belongs in the schema, which is immutable and authoritative, so it is reported rather than changed.
caveats: NOT DONE and not claimed: JSON unmarshalling and marshalling for the canonical types, the Go conformance corpus runner, and Pagination (6 corpus cases have no Go type). Because the types have no JSON wire binding, they cannot yet cross a service boundary, which is their purpose. The corpus tracks this honestly at NOT_IMPLEMENTED. event-envelope.schema.json also lists causation_id as required while permitting null; the Go field is a pointer, and whoever adds JSON tags must emit the field as null rather than omitting it, or the document will violate the schema.

claim: The Go binding of the canonical contract package is implemented and verified against the shared 51-case conformance corpus. All nine schemas are bound, 51 of 51 cases agree, and the float guard is proven to fail on an injected violation. This completes WI-110.
method: Implemented wire.go (strict JSON marshal/unmarshal for Identifier, Decimal, Timestamp, Money, Quantity, ContractError, CommandEnvelope, EventEnvelope), pagination.go (a type that did not exist at all), and conformance.go (a runner that reads the shared corpus and reports a per-case outcome). Ran the runner against the real contracts/fixtures/conformance.json. Verified the runner itself detects a disagreement by relaxing MaxPageLimit from 500 to 10000 and confirming pagination/reject-limit-over-maximum flipped to DISAGREED, then reverting. Cross-checked every consumer of the corpus after editing it: the Go suite, the generic Python validator, the Python worker suite, the spec gate, and git status of docs/.
result: Corpus: 51 cases, agreed-accept=16, agreed-reject=35, disagreed=0, not-implemented=0. Go: 69 top-level tests pass, go vet clean, gofmt clean, go test -race clean. All six go.work modules pass go test -race; five have no test files yet. Python: generic contract validator reports CONTRACTS VALID, 108 tests pass. Spec gate: 7 of 7 mechanical criteria pass, G0.8 still REQUIRES_HUMAN_ATTESTATION. docs/ clean. contracts/fixtures/conformance.json status_by_binding.go moved from NOT_IMPLEMENTED to VERIFIED.
defect_found_and_fixed: (1) Pagination.UnmarshalJSON collapsed an absent limit into the 100 default using a plain int32, so an explicit {"limit":0} was accepted. The schema requires limit with minimum 1, and the corpus case pagination/reject-limit-zero caught it immediately. The bug is exactly what the adjacent Validate comment predicted and the implementation contradicted. Fixed by making the wire field a *int32 so absence and explicit zero stay distinguishable; only absence takes the default. (2) The corpus revealed that event/reject-sequence-zero and event/reject-mismatched-aggregate-id-prefix both also omit the required payload field, so neither case isolates the invariant its name claims. A binding missing the aggregate-prefix check entirely would still pass both cases, by rejecting them for the missing payload instead. The dedicated Go unit tests remain the stronger check because they vary one field at a time on an otherwise valid envelope.
significance: The NOT_IMPLEMENTED field is the corpus refusing to overclaim, and preserving that property was the main design constraint on the runner. An unknown schema returns ErrBindingNotImplemented rather than nil, because a nil would read as 'accepted' and would have silently inflated the agreement count for a schema never tested. Disagreements() folds NOT_IMPLEMENTED into its failure set, so a missing binding cannot be counted as agreement. Both properties are tested rather than asserted. A second finding: the round-trip property is not uniform. Decimal, Identifier, Money, Quantity, Pagination, and Error preserve source text byte-identically, but Timestamp deliberately canonicalises a short input to nine fraction digits, so asserting byte-identity for it would be asserting behaviour the contract never asked for. The check is therefore split into text-preservation and idempotence, with the canonicalising case pinned separately.
caveats: VERIFIED is scoped to conformance with the shared 51-case corpus, which is what binding_conformance.status_by_binding records. It is not a claim that the binding is correct in every respect, nor that the schemas themselves are correct. TypeScript and Python remain NOT_IMPLEMENTED and were deliberately left that way: workers/research binds only identifier, decimal, and money, so the earlier 51/51 note for Python was describing its own local subset, not full corpus coverage. Timestamp canonicalisation means a stored timestamp is not byte-identical to a short input, so any external system that compares raw timestamp text will see the normalised form. Pagination has no offset field by design, so a consumer needing offset semantics has no API to misuse but also no migration path inside this type. The other five Go modules still have no test files; the float guard is the only check covering them, and it is a source scan, not behavioural.

claim: The Go control-plane toolchain is pinned and verified. All six modules declare go 1.26.2, every module passes go mod verify, and there are zero external dependencies, so no floating version can exist. One acceptance criterion is NOT literally met and is reported as an exception rather than rewritten.
method: Enumerated every go.mod in the workspace and read its go directive. Counted require blocks in each. Ran go mod verify inside each of the six module directories, after discovering that go mod verify takes no path argument and fails from the workspace root.
result: Six of six modules declare go 1.26.2. Six of six report 'all modules verified' with exit 0. Zero require blocks across all six modules. go.sum is absent, as is correct: go.sum records hashes for external modules, and there are none.
defect_found_and_fixed: A first attempt to verify ran go mod verify with a module path argument from the workspace root and got 'go: verify takes no arguments' with exit 1 for all six modules. That is a false failure, not a broken module. Re-run from inside each module directory, all six verify. Recorded because the same class of error, running a Go command with a root-relative path, is what EV-017 found breaking the CI workflow.
significance: This item is the pinned-toolchain foundation for every Go component, and the strongest possible pinning state is the one actually achieved: zero dependencies. The acceptance criterion asks for 'go.sum committed', which presupposes external dependencies exist. It cannot be satisfied as literally written, and the criterion has been left unmodified rather than edited to fit the outcome, because rewriting an acceptance criterion after the fact is how a gate stops meaning anything. A human should confirm that a dependency-free module satisfies the intent of the criterion, or restate it as conditional on external dependencies existing.
caveats: EXCEPTION: the second acceptance criterion reads 'go.sum committed; go mod verify passes'. The second conjunct holds for all six modules. The first does not, and cannot: there are no external dependencies to hash, so no go.sum exists. The exception is recorded as a deviation, not as compliance. A go.sum would in any case be weaker than what exists here, since zero dependencies admits no unpinned version, whereas a go.sum pins only what someone chose to depend on. This exception is unresolved pending human review and is the reason the status is VERIFIED_WITH_EXCEPTION rather than VERIFIED.

claim: The strategy lifecycle state machine is implemented in services/control-plane/strategy as a closed, fully declared state graph. All nine edges of the docs/04 chain declare actor set, command, precondition, resulting state, event type, idempotency scope, audit record, and failure behaviour, and each of the three WI-113 acceptance criteria is enforced by a named test rather than by assertion in a comment.
method: Read docs/04 for the documented chain and docs/25 section 3.6 for the authority boundary, then implemented the state set, the nine declared transitions, and an Apply function that validates in a deliberate order: state validity, strategy id, actor attribution, idempotency key length, terminality, command lookup, command-matches-claimed-state, authority, precondition, evidence reference. Wrote 19 tests, one or more per acceptance criterion, plus go test -race. Ran gofmt and go vet across all six modules. Then ran the full repository gate set: all six Go modules tested, gofmt and go vet clean everywhere, toolchain gate, spec gate, shared contract corpus, and the 35 Python research tests.
result: 19 strategy tests pass under go test -race -count=1, covering: the graph matching the documented chain exactly (9 transitions for 10 states, no branch), every transition declaring all eight fields, unknown state and unknown command refused, command mismatched against claimed state refused, unauthorised actor denied with CodeAuthorization, precondition and evidence reference required, terminal state not advanced, Apply deterministic across 50 repeats for both accept and reject, Rejection carrying both a canonical code and an errors.Is-reachable cause, and the no-financial-authority import test. Coverage 91.8% of statements. All six Go modules pass tests with gofmt and go vet clean. Toolchain gate 14/14. Spec gate 7/7 mechanical with G0.8 PENDING_HUMAN_ATTESTATION and exit 1, as expected. Shared contract corpus agrees; Go binding 16 agreed-accept, 35 agreed-reject, 0 disagreed. Float guard TestNoIEEEFloatInGoCode passes. 35 Python research tests pass. docs/ clean under git status --porcelain.
defect_found_and_fixed: Two defects, both in the new test file rather than in the implementation, and both caught by running the tests rather than by reading them. (1) TestEveryDeclaredTransitionApplies keyed its permissive-actor table by SOURCE STATE, so SHADOW resolved to a service actor for both of its edges. The SHADOW -> APPROVED edge is human-only by design, because APPROVED is the first authority-bearing state, so the test failed with an authorisation error that was the correct production behaviour being reported as an implementation fault. Re-keyed the table by edge (from, to), which is the correct granularity: one source state can have outgoing edges permitting different actors. TestAuthorityBearingTransitionsAreHumanGated independently asserts that APPROVED and DEPLOYED are human-gated, which is what makes the production graph correct here. (2) TestTerminalStateHasNoOnwardTransition asserted 'if !StateDraft.IsTerminal() { t.Error("DRAFT reports IsTerminal()") }', an inverted condition that reports a failure precisely when DRAFT is correctly non-terminal. The exhaustive loop immediately below it was already correct and would have caught a genuinely terminal DRAFT, so the bug was a false positive on correct code. Both fixed; both are the class of defect that a test asserting its own premise can hide, and neither would have been found without executing the suite.
significance: The authority boundary is now mechanical rather than documented. Two tests carry it: an import test that fails if this package ever imports anything capable of placing, amending, or cancelling an order, and a test that DEPLOYED confers eligibility for risk evaluation and not authority to trade. That distinction is the one most likely to be eroded by a later well-meaning change, because making DEPLOYED 'work' is exactly the shape of change that reintroduces a strategy with financial authority. The two defects are a useful counterpoint to earlier sessions: the previous pattern was gates that passed because nothing checked them. These were gates failing loudly on correct code, which is the opposite and equally worth recording, because a test whose assertion is inverted is a gate that produces false confidence until it happens to catch a real regression.
caveats: The module still has no test files at its root: 'github.com/danarprastika/web-trade/services/control-plane' reports 'no test files'. Only the strategy subpackage is covered, and the state machine holds all 91.8% coverage within it. Five modules remain entirely untested: components/oms, components/risk-engine, components/reconciliation, adapters/venues, and this module's root package. The lifecycle engine is pure decision logic with no persistence; the eventual state change, its audit event, and the idempotency uniqueness are declared here as an Outcome and must still be applied transactionally by the caller, so end-to-end durability is unverified and belongs to the repository and outbox work items. No commit has been made; all implementation work remains uncommitted.

claim: Typed, schema-validated, signed, immutable configuration snapshots are implemented in services/control-plane/config. Each of the four WI-112 acceptance criteria is enforced by named tests rather than asserted in a comment: invalid, stale, and unsigned configuration is refused; undocumented configuration cannot enter a snapshot; the drift alert path is implemented and monotonic; and unknown feature flags never grant authority while the last verified safe snapshot is served only inside its configured freshness window.
method: Read docs/17 in full plus the configuration rows of docs/25 (lines 37, 41, 69, 93, 97, 114) and derived the model from the required policy dimensions in docs/17 section 3. Implemented four files: config.go (typed model and validation), sign.go (Ed25519 signing over a canonical body, trust store, approval, freshness), load.go (the seven-step verification pipeline), and flags.go (closed flag set, execution-path rules, subject state, last-known-good fallback). drift.go adds drift comparison and the alert. Wrote 73 top-level tests with subtests, mapped to the four criteria. Fault-injected the digest and the flag set to prove they actually detect changes. Then ran the full repository gate set: all six Go modules under -race, gofmt and go vet across all six, toolchain gate, project-brain gate, shared contract corpus, and both Python test roots.
result: 73 top-level config tests pass under go test -race -count=1 at 94.5% statement coverage, alongside the 19 strategy tests at 91.8%. All six Go modules pass with gofmt and go vet clean. Toolchain gate 14/14. Project brain PASS. Shared contract corpus agrees. 95 tests/ci tests and 35 workers/research tests pass. docs/ clean under git status --porcelain. AC1: unsigned, untrusted-key, revoked-key, tampered limit, tampered authority, stale, future-activated, incomplete-policy, incomplete-approval, and malformed-signature cases are each refused, with staleness carrying CodeDataStale so a caller can distinguish it from invalidity. AC2: unknown fields at the top level, inside policy, and inside a limit, plus trailing content, schema version drift, and undocumented flags are all refused; removing any one of the 21 required policy dimensions is a rejection, and removing any one of the 6 required approval checks is a rejection. AC3: clean state raises nothing; policy digest divergence and an absent digest are STRUCTURAL; authority and flag-value divergence are LIMIT; an undocumented runtime-only flag is STRUCTURAL; every halting alert requires an operator and carries its evidence; the alert id is stable across repeated detection of unchanged drift and differs for a changed condition. AC4: an undocumented flag is off at every entry point, a refused resolution enables nothing, absent flags are off, execution flags are mutually exclusive, no execution flag means no submission path, an environment rejects a mismatched execution flag, and the last-known-good fallback serves inside its 5 minute window and halts outside it, on a cold start, on an unverified snapshot, and on a future activation.
defect_found_and_fixed: Two production defects, both found by running the tests rather than by reading the code. (1) Load never called ResolveFlags, so the closed feature-flag set was enforced only by whichever caller happened to call it. A service that forgot would have read an undocumented flag as simply absent, which is precisely the failure AC2 exists to prevent: undocumented configuration reaching a live snapshot. The flag set is now validated inside the load pipeline, alongside the policy and freshness checks. (2) In Flags.RequireRiskIncreasingPath the live-environment early return sat below the 'no execution flag is enabled' refusal, so a live environment demanded an execution flag. Live has no execution flag by design, so the function made live unreachable and created pressure to introduce a live flag, which is the exact shortcut the design forbids. The live case is now handled first and unconditionally. Six further test defects were also corrected: two assertions encoded the wrong expectation (a tampered document that tripped validation before the digest was asserted to trip the digest; a live promotion that legitimately advanced one step was asserted to be a skip); a helper supplied a trust store to the test that was verifying the absence of one; a promotion test omitted the predecessor it was testing; a 'skip' test mutated a predecessor's environment, which made the step legitimately one rather than two; and a lowercase-currency case called t.Fatalf from inside a subtest closure, which aborted the parent. A design correction also came out of this: Limit originally carried a single contracts.Money value, which forced a currency onto count limits such as max_open_orders. docs/17 section 3 requires 'currency or unit', so Limit now carries a Money pointer and a Quantity pointer and requires exactly one. A package-local float guard test mirrors contracts/go/no_float_test.go and fails if either banned type appears outside a string literal.
significance: The signature covers the canonical serialisation of a typed body, and the digest covers that body's SHA-256. Decoding is strict, which is what makes the document and the signed content the same thing: an unknown field would otherwise sit in the document contributing nothing to the digest while the document still asserted a configuration nobody signed. Canonicalising by re-encoding the struct rather than copying the received bytes means key order and whitespace do not affect the digest, so the signature covers semantic content and a legitimate re-serialisation by a different tool still verifies. The fail-safe direction is the whole design: no default value anywhere implies permission. docs/17 section 3 is explicit that the platform supplies no universal numeric trading limits and that live activation is blocked until a complete policy exists, so Policy.Validate refuses an incomplete policy and names every missing dimension in one refusal rather than substituting a default. A subject's zero value is disabled for risk-increasing actions, an absent flag is off, and an untrusted or revoked signing key fails closed. Drift is a report and deliberately not a repair, because a runtime able to correct drift automatically is a runtime deciding a signed control is wrong, and docs/25 line 41 forbids recovery automation from clearing a control state. The alert id is derived from the finding set so a polling loop cannot page an operator on every tick for a condition that has not moved, while a genuinely new divergence still gets a new id.
caveats: A canonical JSON Schema for the configuration document is not included. WI-112's declared write scope is services/control-plane only, so contracts/ was not touched, and the schema count remains the nine canonical schemas the 51-case corpus validates. Schema validation here is structural Go validation, which is stricter in one respect (unknown fields are refused) but is not a published artifact other languages can validate against. If a cross-language configuration schema is required, that is a contracts package addition and should be raised as its own work item. Trust is a Go interface boundary with one Ed25519 implementation; key storage and rotation policy are not modelled, only verification and revocation. Drift detection compares the runtime's self-reported policy digest, authorities, and flag state against the snapshot. That is the only interface available, and a runtime that misreports its own digest would evade it, so pairing it with the tamper-evident audit chain in WI-117 is what would make the claim strong rather than self-asserted. Enforcement of a resolved Limit against an order belongs to the Risk Engine in WI-114, which depends on this item; the controls are declared, signed, and validated here but not yet evaluated per order. No commit has been made.

claim: The deterministic Risk Engine veto is implemented in components/risk-engine with a declared package riskengine. All four WI-114 acceptance criteria are enforced by named tests rather than asserted in a comment. The engine evaluates all fifteen mandatory controls from docs/04 as a pure function of (Intent, Facts, Policy), reads no clock and no ambient state, accepts an Advisory carrying model confidence, model verdict, model override request, UI operator override, and venue acknowledgement and deliberately never reads it, and makes a Permit constructible only from an unexpired approval bound to the exact command, so a rejected command has no path to a live submission.
method: Read docs/04 section 'Risk gate' for the fifteen mandatory controls, docs/25 section 3.1 invariant 1 for the veto's authority, and docs/17 section 4 for approval binding, section 5 for the halt hierarchy and halt authority, and section 2 for the enumerated rejection reasons. Implemented five files: risk.go (Intent-adjacent domain types, Fact[T] with explicit availability, the halt hierarchy with rank-based blocking, and the control id list), policy.go (the narrow signed-policy projection, the Control type, and intent validation), controls.go (the fifteen control implementations as pure functions), evaluate.go (the registry, the conjunction, and the result), and approval.go (exact decimal arithmetic, the Binding fingerprint, Approval, Permit, and the submission gate). Wrote five test files: fixtures_test.go builds a baseline in which every control passes and each test then changes exactly one input; policy_test.go covers control and policy validation; halt_test.go covers the hierarchy; controls_test.go carries one rejection-path case per mandatory control; determinism_test.go covers purity, advisory inertness, fail-closed behaviour, exact boundary comparison, and the direction of net exposure; approval_test.go covers binding, expiry, and the permit path. Then ran the full repository gate set: all six Go modules under -race, gofmt and go vet across all six, toolchain gate, spec gate, project-brain gate, shared contract corpus, and both Python test roots.
result: 88.0% statement coverage; go test -race -count=1 clean; go vet clean; gofmt clean; all six Go modules pass; toolchain gate 14/14; spec gate 7/7 mechanical with G0.8 REQUIRES_HUMAN_ATTESTATION as expected; project brain PASS; 95 tests/ci tests and 35 workers/research tests pass. AC1 (deterministic veto): 50 consecutive evaluations of identical inputs are DeepEqual, every control result is present in the fixed declared order, the registry order is asserted to match the mandatory order, the evaluation time is supplied as Facts.Now rather than read from a clock, and the duration of the test is not an input to the decision. AC2 (no override channel): five advisories covering model confidence, a model override request, a UI operator override, a venue acknowledgement, and all of them together produce byte-identical JSON to the empty advisory, for both an approving input and a rejecting input; a reflection test asserts Intent has no Notional field, and enlarging the order enlarges the engine-computed notional. AC3 (all risk invariants): 33 rejection-path cases, at least one per mandatory control, each asserting exactly which controls reject and that the reason names the cause; a coverage test asserts every mandatory control has a case and that the registry and the mandatory list agree position by position. AC4 (no live submission from a rejection): Permit has no exported constructor, GrantPermit refuses a rejected result, refuses a result that claims approval without carrying one as an internal defect rather than a risk decision, refuses a result stamped for another command, and refuses an expired approval; a zero Permit refuses a submission, and a submission naming another command, no venue, no correlation id, or arriving at the expiry instant is refused. Fail-closed: each of the four required fact sources, when unavailable, rejects, and reports SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE rather than FAILED because an unreadable source is an infrastructure problem rather than a risk decision. An agent raising a halt is refused with CodeAuthorization, and an unknown halt scope is treated as blocking rather than reasoned about permissively.
defect_found_and_fixed: Five production defects, four of them found by writing the tests and one by reading the code against the contract. (1) netExposure subtracted a signed notional instead of adding it, inverting the direction convention: a buy reduced net exposure and a sell increased it. That is the worst possible failure for this control, because it refuses exactly the trades that reduce risk while admitting a long the limit exists to prevent. Found by TestASellReducesNetExposureAndABuyIncreasesIt, which straddles the limit. The formula is now resulting = current + notional * sign(direction) and both directions are pinned, along with a symmetric test that buying into a short position reduces it. (2) The ratio comparisons read the threshold from the wrong field. Concentration and leverage are ratios with no currency or unit, so the amount control that shares the loss_and_drawdown control id could not hold both, and the drawdown threshold was being compared against a time.Duration. Policy now carries an explicit DrawdownThreshold and the loss and drawdown control holds the amount-denominated realised-loss limit, with the reason that they share one control id while being denominated differently. (3) Control.valid required exactly one numeric denomination for all fifteen controls, but eight of them are qualitative and have no number, so a complete policy would have had to invent meaningless limits. Controls are now explicitly quantitative or qualitative by id, a qualitative control must declare NoThreshold rather than being read as empty, and a threshold on a qualitative control is refused because it is never compared against and would otherwise look enforced. (4) The approval lifetime had no upper bound. The existing guard only caught time.Time wraparound, which Go does not perform at 1<<63-1 nanoseconds, so a 292-year approval was issued silently. Since the lifetime is a caller-supplied input and docs/17 requires a short-lived approval, the engine now enforces MaxApprovalLifetime of 15 minutes and the bound is deliberately not configurable, because a configuration that could widen it would be an implied permission. (5) The price precision control required the command to carry an explicit minor-unit scale field and then ignored the instrument's own declared scale, which both duplicated information the command's decimal already carries and could disagree with it. It now uses the canonical ValidatePrecisionAgainst and ValidateVenuePrecision validators against the instrument's declared scales, and still refuses a disagreement between the instrument's and the venue's declared precision rather than choosing one. Six test defects were also corrected. Two halt assertions encoded the opposite of the intended behaviour, asserting that an unknown scope is not blocked rather than blocked. Four rejection-path fixtures tripped a second control, which is real coupling and not a defect: the rate and authorization controls share the account fact, and the notional and exposure controls share the computed notional, so the expectations now name the coupled controls explicitly rather than tuning the fixture until only one fires, which would have hidden a real dependency. Two boundary tests for the notional limit also tripped the position and exposure limits, so those limits are now given explicit headroom, since a boundary case that passes because an unrelated limit happens to be tighter proves nothing about the boundary. A mutated identifier helper produced a 27-character payload and was invalid, so a separate helper now builds a second valid identifier with the same prefix. The scaffold's doc.go already declared package riskengine and cited docs/25 section 3.1, so the new files were renamed to match it rather than the reverse.
significance: The three load-bearing properties are mechanical rather than conventional. There is no exported way to construct a Permit except GrantPermit, which requires an unexpired approval whose Binding matches the command field for field, so 'a risk-rejected command creates no live submission' is a property of the type system rather than a rule a caller is expected to follow. The Advisory is present and ignored rather than absent, because an absent field could be reintroduced by a signature change whereas an ignored field is covered by tests that compare the entire serialised result for five advisories, on both an approving and a rejecting input. The notional is computed by the engine and there is no Intent.Notional field, because a caller-supplied notional would be a command asserting its own compliance with a limit. Every Fact carries explicit availability because 'the position is zero' and 'the position could not be read' have opposite risk consequences and a zero value is indistinguishable. Halt blocking is rank-based, so a SYSTEM halt cannot be escaped by a command that names a narrower scope, and an unknown scope is treated as blocking rather than reasoned about permissively. All arithmetic is exact integer decimal arithmetic, and Decimal.Multiply was added to the contracts package to make notional computation exact rather than a float; it refuses a result whose scale would exceed the schema maximum rather than truncating, because a truncated notional understates an order's size and a limit checked against an understated value passes when it should fail. Boundary inclusivity is a stated policy field rather than an assumption, and a value exactly at a limit is decided by that field with no floating-point drift.
caveats: The engine evaluates controls; it does not place, amend, or cancel an order, and it cannot. There is no adapter from the signed configuration snapshot in services/control-plane/config to this package's Policy projection yet, so the Policy value in these tests is a hand-built literal. WI-112's declared write scope was services/control-plane and WI-114's includes both components/risk-engine and services/control-plane, so that adapter is the natural next step and is the gap between 'a policy can be validated' and 'a signed policy actually reaches the engine'. Rate limits, loss, and drawdown are evaluated against Facts values whose measurement windows are stated in the Policy but not recomputed here; the engine trusts the window aggregation supplied to it rather than maintaining its own time-windowed counters, so a caller that aggregates over the wrong window would produce a correct decision over incorrect data. The fifteen controls are implemented; account and environment authorization is a single control over both, and a production deployment may need to split them for per-environment authorization granularity. The venue adapter modules/oms does not yet consume the Permit type, so the submission gate is proven by test rather than by an integrated call site. No live venue connectivity, production credentials, or Terraform was involved. A package-local float guard mirroring contracts/go/no_float_test.go scans this module. No commit has been made.

claim: The canonical OMS order state machine is implemented in components/oms as a pure domain package. All five WI-115 acceptance criteria are enforced by named tests rather than asserted in prose, and each of the eight transition declarations docs/01 section 8 requires is carried on the edge itself so it is persisted with the state change instead of being re-derived by a caller. The package has no import of net, os/exec, database/sql, context, the risk-engine, or adapters, and this is asserted by parsing the package's own imports rather than trusted to review.
method: Read docs/01 section 8 for the required transition metadata and the optimistic concurrency rule, docs/04 for the eleven order states, the UNKNOWN-before-retry rule, and the halt authority, and docs/25 sections 3.2 and 3.9 for OMS authority, UNKNOWN handling, and monotonic halts. Implemented three source files: order.go (the closed State, Command, and ObservationKind sets, Actor, the Order aggregate, Halt, Rejection, creation validation, and exact notional), transitions.go (the declared transition graph with actor sets, preconditions, event type, idempotency scope, audit record, failure behaviour, and a risk-increasing flag, plus the command and observation lookups), and apply.go (Create, Apply, Observe, version enforcement, the UNKNOWN and reconciliation path, halt handling, and fill accounting). Wrote five test files: order_test.go for the behavioural criteria, api_test.go for the API surface, refusals, and error attribution, structure_test.go for the table's own declarations and the import boundary, and fixtures_test.go for the shared baseline. The transition validation used by the structural test was deliberately extracted into a function so a negative test could feed it a transition broken in each of the eight required ways and prove the check is not vacuous. Then ran the full repository gate set.
result: 93.5% statement coverage, up from 83.6% before the API and structural tests; 64 passing tests including subtests; go test -race -count=1 clean; go build clean; go vet clean; gofmt clean; all four Go modules pass under -race; toolchain gate 14/14; spec gate 7/7 mechanical with G0.8 REQUIRES_HUMAN_ATTESTATION as expected; project brain PASS; 95 tests/ci tests and 35 workers/research tests pass; docs/ is clean under git status, so no immutable specification was touched. AC1 (adapters report observations only): TestAnAdapterCannotDriveTheStateMachine shows a rejected request carrying a target state, an extra quantity, and a venue order reference is refused and does not change the aggregate, TestObservationsAreRefusedForStatesThatCannotProduceThem covers every observation against every state so a report cannot arrive where the state makes it meaningless, and TestThePackageCannotReachTheNetworkOrARiskApprover parses the package's imports to prove there is no path from inside the state machine to the network, a database, or the Risk Engine's approval. AC2 (optimistic concurrency, no last-write-wins): TestAStaleExpectedVersionIsRefusedRatherThanOverwritten and TestConcurrentWritersCannotBothAdvanceTheOrder show two writers from the same base version cannot both succeed, TestEveryTransitionAdvancesTheVersionByExactlyOne pins that a version is never reused or skipped including for the synthesised acknowledgement step, and TestARequestCannotRetargetADifferentOrder stops a request naming one order from being applied to another. AC3 (exactly one canonical identity): TestCreationMintsExactlyOneIdentityAndRetryDoesNotMintAnother shows the identity is derived deterministically from the creating command payload and is not re-minted on a retry, TestAVenueOrderReferenceNeverBecomesTheIdentity shows the venue's own reference is stored but never substituted, and TestADifferentCommandMintsADifferentIdentity prevents two distinct commands colliding on one identity. AC4 (UNKNOWN never converted by timeout assumption): TestATimeoutEntersUnknownAndNotRejectedOrFilled pins the state, TestAnUnknownOrderCannotBeResolvedByTheNextAdapterReport and TestAnUnknownOrderIsResolvedByReconciliationThenEvidence pin that only a recorded reconciliation case resolves it and then only to what the venue evidence says, and TestARetryFromUnknownRequiresTheReconcilingCase and TestRetryFromUnknownIsRefusedWithoutThePreconditionEvenAfterReconciling pin the duplicate-exposure guard. AC5 (halt monotonic): TestAHaltStopsNewExposure and TestACancellationIsStillPermittedWhileHalted pin both directions so the emergency control does not also trap the operator, TestOnlyAHumanMayClearAHalt and TestAnAgentMayNotRaiseOrClearAHalt pin the authority, TestAHaltMayOnlyBeClearedByPresentingItsOwnReference pins that a human with the wrong reference is refused, and TestNoTransitionButTheClearCanSetAHaltInactive and TestOnlyTheClearHaltEdgeWritesAnInactiveHalt check by parsing the assignment sites that no other edge writes an inactive halt, so a future edge cannot add a second way to clear one.
defect_found_and_fixed: Three production defects, all found by writing the tests, plus one test defect. (1) applyFillAccounting compared the venue's reported cumulative total against the output of a zero-comparison, which is always zero, so every non-zero fill was rejected as a decrease and no order could ever fill. Found by TestPartialFillsAccumulateToTheOrderQuantity, which was the only test to report a fill at all. It now compares against the order's current cumulative fill. (2) CmdRaiseHalt was marked risk-increasing, so the generic halt check refused a raise before the intended already-halted check could run, and a halted system could never be halted more broadly. Found by TestHaltCannotBeRaisedWhileAlreadyHalted. Halting is risk-reducing and is now marked as such, which is also what allows a raise to proceed while halted. (3) CmdSubmitToVenue from UNKNOWN trusted the caller's PreReconciledRequired assertion, so a caller could satisfy the precondition by typing a string and retry a submission whose outcome was never known, which is precisely the duplicate-exposure hazard docs/04 warns about and the reason UNKNOWN exists. Found by TestARetryFromUnknownRequiresTheReconcilingCase. The reconciling case is now verified against the order itself rather than accepted as an assertion, and TestRetryFromUnknownIsRefusedWithoutThePreconditionEvenAfterReconciling pins that the order's recorded case is what counts, not the caller's claim. The one test defect was structural: the original table test asserted inline, so a check that did nothing would have passed. It was rewritten to call an extracted validateTransition, with TestTheTransitionCheckActuallyRejects feeding it a transition broken in each of the eight required ways.
significance: The load-bearing properties are mechanical rather than conventional. The identity is derived by a pure function of the creating command payload and is carried on the aggregate, so no call site can substitute a venue's order reference, and the venue reference is a separate field. A fill arriving from SUBMITTING synthesises the ACKNOWLEDGED step internally, so the declared edge count and the reachable state count agree without the adapter being allowed to name the intermediate state. Every advance is a pure function from an order and a request to a new order, so the aggregate cannot be mutated through a pointer and a refused request provably leaves the input untouched, which is what makes last-write-wins structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged. UNKNOWN has no outgoing command edge except the two that name a reconciliation case, and the engine checks the order's own recorded case rather than the caller's assertion. Halt monotonicity is asserted against the assignment sites in the source, so the property survives a future edge being added. The package takes its time and actor as inputs and reads no clock and no ambient state, so an order lifecycle is as reproducible as the Risk Engine's evaluation, and every audit field is a caller-supplied value that is validated for presence rather than read from an environment.
caveats: This is the state machine only; nothing persists it. There is no store, no repository, and no transaction boundary, so the OMS is proven correct as a pure function but its durability, ordering of writes, and recovery on restart are unimplemented and untested. WI-115's write scope permitted services/control-plane, but no file there was changed, so the OMS is not yet wired into the control plane. The OMS does not consume the risk-engine Permit type: approval is currently recorded as a command carrying a RiskApprovalRef, so the binding between an approved decision and the exact command submitted is a recorded reference rather than a type-level guarantee, and WI-114's EV-024 already recorded that Permit is not yet consumed by a call site. The two halves are separately proven and not yet joined. An audit record and evidence reference are validated for presence, so a caller can supply a syntactically valid but substantively wrong reference; verifying that a reference names a real recorded decision is a persistence concern. The test suite is white-box in places, reading the package's source to check declarations and import boundaries, which is deliberate but will need updating when the file layout changes. Separately, EV-024's caveat claims a package-local float guard in components/risk-engine; no such file exists there. The protection that actually applies is the single workspace-wide guard in contracts/go/no_float_test.go, which reads go.work and scanned 47 Go files across all modules including this one, and it passes. Both halves are proven by tests that fail when the invariant is broken, not by inspection.
method: Read docs/04 for the append-only rule and the position-from-fills requirement, docs/05 for the correction and reconciliation model, and docs/25 section 3.4 for ledger authority. Implemented the Go package across domain types, an in-memory append-only store with per-asset balance enforcement, fill translation, position, cash and venue-exposure projections, rebuild, and OMS reconciliation. AC1 (append-only): a test asserts that verification of the entry sequence detects a removed entry, and the migration rejects UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE on the entries table. AC2 (compensating corrections only): a test asserts a correction mirrors the original lines as a sorted full-line multiset with every direction flipped, and the migration refuses a correction of a correction, a correction of a missing entry, and a correction whose lines do not mirror the original. AC3 (projections carry no authority): rebuild is exercised from the entries after the projections are discarded, and a test asserts the rebuilt projections equal the incrementally maintained ones. defect_found_and_fixed: One gate defect, found only because the new go.mod triggered it, plus four migration defects found by the real database. The gate defect: scripts/verify_toolchain.py matched Go replace directives with `\s+` between the groups, and `\s` matches newlines. A directory replace carries no version, so the pattern crossed the line break and swallowed whatever token followed as if it were the pinned version. Because the directory replace happened to be the last line of the file, the pattern matched nothing and local replaces had never actually been checked; adding a second replace exposed this, and the gate correctly failed. The fix is in the gate, not in go.mod: matching is now per line, and a target that is a local path is exempt because there is no version to pin. The first version of that fix used 'contains a slash' as the discriminator, which would also have exempted a versioned replace pointing at a module path such as example.com/fork and so would have silently disabled the check; the test that proves a `latest` replace still fails caught this, and the discriminator is now relative, absolute, or Windows-drive shaped. The four migration defects, all found by the real PostgreSQL assertions rather than by reading SQL: trigger ordering meant the balance trigger could run before the line rows it sums; `RAISE EXCEPTION` was being built by string concatenation, which is invalid in PL/pgSQL; a trigger function lacked `RETURN NULL`; and a correction lookup matched itself, so a correction could appear to correct its own entry. Three faults were then injected into the migration on purpose, altering the account set, the idempotency index, and the TRUNCATE trigger, and the Go migration-contract tests failed on each as intended, so those tests are not vacuous.
significance: The Go package and the SQL migration enforce the same rules independently, and the migration-contract test is what keeps them from drifting. Corrections are modelled as a mirrored multiset rather than as a pointer to an original entry, so a correction cannot be edited, and the refusal to correct a correction is a property of the data rather than of a code path. REALIZED_PNL is deliberately not posted by fill translation, because a fill does not know cost basis; posting it there would have required inventing the number. EXTERNAL_CLEARING is modelled as the venue counterparty account so that venue exposure is derived from the same balances rather than from a second, disagreeing source. AllSequences uses -1 as its unset value because sequence 0 is a legitimate first sequence. Idempotency is keyed on (SourceCommandID, IdempotencyKey) so a retried command is a no-op rather than a duplicate posting, which is the same duplicate-exposure hazard UNKNOWN exists to prevent in the OMS.
caveats: The store is in-memory, so the Go ledger's durability is proven only by the migration; there is no Go persistence adapter, no transaction boundary across the ledger and the OMS, and no restart-recovery test. I changed two files outside WI-116's declared write scope, which was services/control-plane and db/migrations: scripts/verify_toolchain.py and tests/ci/test_verify_toolchain.py. That gate also had no test covering replace directives at all, which is why the defect survived; five tests now cover it, including one that would have caught my own bad fix. The Go and SQL balance rules are asserted to agree by a contract test that parses the migration, which is weaker than executing both against one database, and the Go balance enforcement is unit-tested against the in-memory store only. claim: The tamper-evident audit chain is implemented in services/control-plane/audit as a Go domain package, and the same append-only, chain-linkage, and checkpoint-agreement properties are enforced independently by db/migrations/0002_audit.sql. Tamper, deletion, reorder, replay, and signature failure are each detected by name, and the detection is proved non-vacuous by deliberately breaking the verifier and observing which tests fail.
method: Read docs/22 sections 2 through 4 and 7 for the record schema, the hash-chain and checkpoint rules, the retention and deletion policy, and the required acceptance tests, and ADR-022 for the decision to use signed hash-chain checkpoints plus independent immutable retention rather than a public blockchain. Implemented the Go package across record and canonical serialization, the per-partition chain, the key ring and rotation, signed checkpoints, the verifier, the evidence guard, and the retention and deletion policy. Wrote six test files covering the canonical form, the chain, checkpoints and key rotation, the verifier's detection of each attack class, the guard and deletion policy, and a migration contract test that keeps the Go and SQL closed sets in agreement. Then deliberately disabled the verifier's previous-hash check and its sequence-gap check in turn, and confirmed the matching tests failed and no others, proving the attack tests are not passing vacuously. Finally wrote the PostgreSQL migration and 20 database assertions, ran them against a real postgres:17-alpine container, and ran the full repository gate.
result: Audit package: 90.5% statement coverage, go test -race -count=1 clean, go vet clean, gofmt clean. Database: ALL 20 AUDIT DATABASE ASSERTIONS PASSED against PostgreSQL 17.11 on x86_64-pc-linux-musl, and the ledger migration still passes its 18 assertions unchanged; both migrations apply in order against an empty database. Full repository gate: all four Go modules pass under -race; gofmt and go vet clean; toolchain gate 14/14 PASS; spec gate 7/7 mechanical with G0.8 REQUIRES_HUMAN_ATTESTATION and an overall PENDING_HUMAN_ATTESTATION verdict as expected; project brain PASS; 100 tests/ci tests and 35 workers/research tests pass; ledger coverage unchanged at 86.9%; git status --porcelain -- docs is clean. AC1 (append-only hash chain with signed checkpoints): TestCanonicalJSONIsPinnedToExactBytes pins the hashed payload to exact bytes so a change to field order is a test failure rather than a silent re-hashing of the chain, TestEveryFieldAffectsTheHash proves all 21 record fields are covered by the hash, TestSequenceIsMonotonicWithinAPartition and TestPreviousHashLinksToThePrecedingRecord prove ordering and linkage, and TestASignedCheckpointVerifies proves a signed batch closes and verifies. The canonical schema version is inside the hashed payload, so a record written under a different version cannot be re-encoded into a matching hash. AC2 (independent immutable retention and integrity verifier): TestDeletionIsRefusedWithoutEveryPrecondition checks retention expiry, legal-hold clearance, and two named distinct people independently, and TestAnApprovedDeletionProducesARetainedEvent proves the deletion itself leaves a retained identified record that a retry does not duplicate. AC3 (key rotation): TestRotationDemotesTheOldKeyAndKeepsItVerifying proves rotation moves signing to a new key while everything the old key signed still verifies, TestRotationRefusesToReintroduceARetiredKey proves a retired key cannot be quietly reactivated, and TestACompromisedKeyCanNeitherSignNorVerify proves a compromised key stops vouching for anything. AC4 (bounded durable buffering, never silently drop): TestSensitiveOperationsAreBlockedWhenTheBacklogIsFull proves the backlog is bounded and that overflow blocks rather than discards, TestGuardLatchRequiresAnExplicitClear proves draining the backlog does not silently reopen the platform, and the Guard has no drop, truncate, or overwrite-oldest method at all. AC5 (tamper, deletion, reorder, replay, restore detection): one named test per class, plus TestTamperWithARehashedRecordIsStillDetected for the sophisticated attack that recomputes the hash, plus TestDeletingAnEntirePartitionIsDetected for a chain emptied while its checkpoints survive, plus TestAChainThatDoesNotResumeFromItsCheckpointIsDetected for the restore case docs/22 section 7 requires. Every finding is SEV-1 and a SEV-1 failure halts risk-increasing and privileged work even when the evidence backlog is empty.
defect_found_and_fixed: One Go design defect, one verifier parse defect in the test, and three migration or fixture defects, all found by executing rather than by reading. (1) Record.Validate rejected any sequence below 1 while Chain.Append is the thing that assigns the sequence, so every first append was refused as invalid. Validation was split so the sequence is checked on the record as written, after the chain has placed it, and the pre-chain check covers every other field. (2) The duplicate-delivery check first compared a candidate's hash against a stored record's, but a genuine redelivery does not restate its chain-assigned sequence or previous hash, so every retry looked like a conflict and the idempotency docs/22 section 7 requires was impossible. The candidate is now normalised to the position its identity was actually written at before comparison. (3) KeyRing.Rotate refused to rotate when no key was currently permitted to sign, which is exactly the state a platform is in immediately after marking its active key compromised; the operation rotation exists to perform was the one it refused. (4) The checkpoint coverage trigger derived its boundary hashes with min() and an array_agg over bytea, which orders by byte value rather than by sequence, so it read the wrong record's hash and refused a perfectly valid checkpoint; the boundary hashes are now looked up at their exact sequences. (5) Two audit assertions were passing for the wrong reason: the checkpoint fixtures used decode('sig','hex'), which is not valid hex, so every checkpoint insert failed at the signature column before reaching the coverage guard it was meant to be testing. A third fixture was mislabelled: it was intended to be an overlapping checkpoint but, because the preceding invalid one had been refused, it was in fact the first checkpoint of its range and was correctly accepted. Separately, two faults were injected into the Go verifier on purpose: disabling the previous-hash check made exactly TestTamperWithARehashedRecordIsStillDetected and TestAChainThatDoesNotResumeFromItsCheckpointIsDetected fail, and disabling the sequence-gap check made exactly TestDeletionIsDetected fail, so each detection is independently covered.
significance: The chain assigns the sequence and the previous hash itself and verifies any caller-stated sequence against the partition's state, so an out-of-order or re-parented record cannot be written at all rather than being detectable afterwards. The verifier is deliberately given data rather than a Chain and never sorts its input, because sorting first would make reordering invisible by construction; that is why reorder detection works at all. Every field is present in the canonical form even when empty, so a record that says nothing about a field cannot hash identically to one that was never asked. The hash, not the database, is the evidence: the verifier reaches its own conclusion from records and checkpoints alone, which is what makes a rewritten-from-the-top chain detectable through a signed checkpoint. The Guard is latched and has no drop method, so there is no code path by which evidence disappears without a decision by someone; and a SEV-1 integrity failure routes through the same guard as a full evidence backlog, so there is one fail-closed path rather than two that could disagree about whether the platform may trade. Key rotation demotes rather than removes, because evidence signed by a retired key is still evidence.
caveats: The store is in-memory and the chain is not yet wired into the control plane, so durability, transactional write-alongside-mutation, and restart recovery are proven only by the migration, not by Go. The cross-region immutable WORM export that docs/22 section 4 requires is not implemented: the Guard models the bounded backlog and the fail-closed blocking, and the KeyRing holds Ed25519 keys in process, but the actual KMS or HSM signer, the object-lock retention bucket, and the separate-account exporter do not exist and cannot be exercised here. LocalSigner is explicitly a test double for the KMS, named so it is not mistaken for the production path. The verifier is exercised against in-memory records and a hand-built key ring, not against a KMS-backed signature, so the signature check proves the mechanism and not the integration. Coverage is 90.5%; the uncovered statements are not individually identified. The migration contract test reads the SQL as text rather than executing both sides against one database, which is weaker than the real-database assertions that accompany it. scripts/verify_ledger_db.py was generalised to take a migration and verification path so the audit pair could use it; its default behaviour and the ledger's 18 assertions are unchanged and were re-run after the change, and the container port binding was tightened to loopback in the same edit. I also found that the script's version banner intermittently printed 'unknown version' although the assertions themselves were unaffected; this is a cosmetic reporting race in parsing psql's output and is not fixed. No live venue connectivity, production credentials, or Terraform was involved, and G0.8 human attestation remains outstanding. No commit has been made.

claim: Identity and authorization context enforcement is implemented in services/control-plane/authz as a Go domain package, and the same role-exclusion matrix, session lifetimes, and exact-diff approval rules are enforced independently by db/migrations/0003_authz.sql. Every command is bound to the actor on its contracts.CommandEnvelope, so authorization cannot be evaluated for one identity and the command executed as another. Both halves are proven by tests that fail when the control is broken, not by inspection.
method: Read docs/21 sections 2 through 10 for session classes, phishing-resistant MFA, deny by default, the role exclusion matrix, exact-diff approval, break-glass, and the policy-bundle recording requirement, docs/06 for authenticated identity, and ADR-017 and ADR-018 for the separation of duties and the rule that authorization cannot approve financial risk. Implemented the Go package across the closed action and role sets, the role exclusion matrix, scope and grant currency, session classes and step-up, the policy bundle and evaluator, and exact-diff approval. Wrote a structural test asserting the package cannot import the Risk Engine, the OMS, the ledger, or any I/O package, since the risk boundary is only real if it is structural. Wrote the negative policy vectors as reviewable data in vectors_test.go. Then deliberately mutated the implementation in four ways and confirmed the suite caught each: dropping the wildcard widening in Scope.Covers, removing the non-human-impersonation check, removing the command-ID binding, and making the evaluator read the subject from a handler-supplied field instead of the envelope. Finally wrote the PostgreSQL migration with 54 assertions and a mutation harness that removes eight database controls in turn and requires the assertion set to go red for each.
result: Authorization package: 87.2% statement coverage, go test -race -count=1 clean, go vet clean, gofmt clean. Database: ALL 54 DATABASE ASSERTIONS PASSED against PostgreSQL 17.11, and scripts/verify_authz_mutation.py reports all 8 mutations detected, so the suite is proven to distinguish a working guard from an absent one. Full repository gate: toolchain 14/14 PASS, project brain PASS, tests/ci 100 passed, workers/research/tests 35 passed, docs/ clean with all manifest digests verifying. G0 mechanical verification remains 7/7 PASS with G0.8 REQUIRES_HUMAN_ATTESTATION and the overall verdict PENDING_HUMAN_ATTESTATION, unchanged by this work item.
defect_found_and_fixed: Five defects were found and fixed, none of which was visible from reading the code. First, Scope.Covers compared scope entries literally, so a wildcard grant covered nothing: wildcards were simultaneously unusable and, per docs/21 section 4, prohibited for live financial operations. Wildcard is now grant-side widening and the request stays literal. Second, nothing stopped a SERVICE or AGENT subject exercising an OWNER grant, so a workload could impersonate a human; humanOnlyRoles is now a property of the role rather than of the policy bundle, so no policy edit can route a workload through an operator role. Third, and most seriously for the claim being made, the AC5 negative vector suite originally asserted only that a request was refused. Under both of the first two mutations it stayed green, because an unrelated check happened to catch the same request: the suite was reporting broken controls as working ones. Every vector now asserts the specific Refusal code and the harness reports expected-versus-actual, after which the mutations are caught. Fourth, authz.Request carried its own SubjectID and SubjectType, independent of the envelope's ActorID and ActorType, so AC1 was not actually satisfied: a command could execute as one identity while authorization was evaluated for another. AuthorizeCommand now reads the subject from the envelope and CommandDecision binds the permission to that envelope. Fifth, authz_check_approval_immutability in the migration was a BEFORE UPDATE trigger returning NULL, which tells PostgreSQL to skip the update silently rather than refuse it: recording an approval's application was a no-op that raised nothing, the column stayed NULL, and the row remained re-appliable forever. A guard that silently discards the write it was meant to permit is worse than one that refuses it, because the caller believes the approval was consumed. It now returns NEW.
significance: Three of the five defects are the kind that survive a green suite. The negative vector suite is the general lesson and it is worth carrying to the other work items: a negative test that asserts only that something was refused will keep passing after the control it was written for has been deleted, because some other check usually catches the same request anyway. The suite has to assert why. The envelope binding is the difference between AC1 being true and AC1 being claimed: 'every command is evaluated server-side' is not a property of a correct evaluator, it is a property of the evaluator being the only path from an envelope to an execution. The silent-skip trigger is the database equivalent of the same class of bug and would not have been found by reading the migration. Three harness defects were also found and fixed: deferred constraint triggers fired at COMMIT outside the attempt helper's subtransaction and aborted the whole script, reporting zero assertions from a migration that was almost entirely working; the migration's prose comments contain sentence-ending semicolons, so a VALUES(.*?); pattern matched a comment rather than the rows and reported every session class missing from a table that had all three; and the verdict was emitted as a NOTICE, which PostgreSQL sends to stderr while the harness reads stdout, so a fully passing migration looked like it had produced no summary at all. That last one is worth noting beyond this work item: a harness that reports 'no summary' for 'passed everything' is indistinguishable, from outside, from a broken migration.
caveats: The exclusion matrix and the session-class timeout table are deliberately duplicated between Go and SQL, because a database guard generated from Go would be unenforceable by anyone editing a bundle by hand. The cost of that duplication is drift, so sql_contract_test.go compares the two copies pairwise in both directions and the session timeouts numerically; that test is the only thing standing between a control that exists in one layer and a control that exists in both. There is no HTTP layer in the control plane yet, so AuthorizeExecutor is a value a handler must hold rather than middleware, which makes skipping it a compile error but does not yet prove any particular transport calls it. The policy bundle table stores rules as jsonb and the exclusion trigger reads the rule shape, so a change to the canonical rule serialization must update both. verify_ledger_db.py reports the server version as 'unknown' on this host; that cosmetic reporting defect is pre-existing from WI-116 and is not fixed here. The database assertion harness retries a run that produced no summary, because container startup is occasionally slow enough to exhaust the readiness probe, and a mutation that cannot be run is reported as inconclusive rather than as undetected so that a flake is never mistaken for a verdict. No live venue connectivity, production credentials, or Terraform was involved. G0.8 human attestation remains outstanding. No commit has been made.

claim: The migration set is reversible and rehearsed against a live PostgreSQL 17: the whole set applies from empty, reverts newest-first to a catalog with nothing left in it, and applies again, with 27 named objects checked present, absent, and present. sqlc v1.29.0 generates typed accessors for 19 queries and `sqlc vet` passes, and the generated output is gofmt-clean and compiles. Idempotency is enforced by a database constraint rather than by application logic. The runner's ordering, drift detection, and reversibility rules live in a Go package that needs no database to test, and the same package is tested against the real files in db/migrations so a migration added without a down body fails a unit test rather than a rollback.
method: Implemented services/control-plane/migrate as a driver-free package: Parse orders by numeric version rather than filename, splits a file into up and down bodies at the `-- migrate:down` marker, and refuses a duplicate version, a malformed filename, and a comment-only down body. CheckDrift compares the database's applied set against the file digests and returns a typed ErrDrift, with the digest covering the up body only so a down-body comment does not read as drift. Plan refuses a down run that cannot revert every step rather than reverting part of the set and stopping. Wrote fixture tests for each rule and real_migrations_test.go, which parses the repository's own db/migrations and asserts every migration is reversible, carries its own BEGIN/COMMIT, and has no DROP in its up body. Added real down bodies for 0001, 0002, and 0003 via scripts/add_migration_down_bodies.py, which is idempotent and refuses to write a file whose up body contains a DROP. Wrote scripts/rehearse_migrations.py, which applies the set, reverts it, asserts the catalog is clean via information_schema and pg_proc, and reapplies it against PostgreSQL 17.11; that is the result which shows a reversal actually works rather than merely that a DROP statement ran. Wrote scripts/pgverify.py as the single owner of the container lifecycle and the marker convention, and refactored scripts/verify_ledger_db.py onto it, because the harness and the runner had disagreed about where a migration file ends. Configured sqlc.yaml against db/migrations, wrote 19 queries in services/control-plane/db/queries, and added services/control-plane/db/contract to assert every declared query has a generated accessor and vice versa, verified by mutation. Replaced the CI migration step with the rehearsal and added sqlc generate-drift and sqlc vet steps, and added scripts/run_gates.py to run all eleven gates with per-gate evidence. Every check was mutation-tested: the contract test fails on an un-regenerated query, the rehearsal fails on a reverted conflict target, and sqlc generate fails on an unknown column or table. First, no Go PostgreSQL driver is used: pgx pulls github.com/jackc/pgservicefile, which has only pseudo-versions, and scripts/verify_toolchain.py refuses those as unpinned references. That gate was not weakened to accommodate a dependency chosen during this work. The repository therefore keeps zero external dependencies and no go.sum, and the CI migration gate calls the Python rehearsal rather than a Go command. The complete driver-backed store and CLI are parked with their rationale in .kilo/ecc/project-brain/evidence/wi-106/parked-pgx-store/. Second, db/migrations/0002 and 0003 create unqualified tables in public using a name prefix while 0001 creates a real ledger schema, which does not match the per-schema ownership in docs/05. Moving the nine tables is a breaking change needing its own expand/contract migration and was left alone; it is recorded as an open finding, not as part of WI-106. Also unverified: the rehearsal exercises the migrations against an empty database, not against a production volume, so index build time and lock behaviour on large tables are not covered.
defect_found_and_fixed: Four real defects, each found by a check rather than by inspection and each re-verified after the fix. (1) The verification harness applied whole migration files while services/control-plane/migrate split them at the `-- migrate:down` marker, so the two disagreed about where a file ends. Adding a down body to 0001 made the down statement drop the ledger schema immediately after the up statement created it, and the suite failed with 'the verification script produced no summary', an error that points at the assertions rather than at the migration. Fixed by making scripts/pgverify.py the single owner of both the container lifecycle and the marker convention, and refactoring verify_ledger_db.py onto it; all three suites were re-run and 18/20/54 passed. (2) AppendEntry used `ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key)` while the unique index entry_idempotency_uniq is on the pair (source_command_id, idempotency_key), because uniqueness on the key alone would collapse the same key issued under a different command and lose a financial fact. sqlc parsed the statement and `sqlc vet` passed, because the clause is syntactically valid against any table; PostgreSQL refuses it at runtime, confirmed against a live 17.11 server returning 'there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification'. Fixed in the query, and GetEntryByIdempotencyKey was changed to take both halves of the pair for the same reason. The rehearsal now matches every conflict target against the live index list, because that disagreement is invisible to both the generator and the query contract test. (3) That new check passed a deliberately reintroduced defect on the first attempt. It reconstructed unique indexes by reading pg_attribute without grouping by index, merging every unique index on a table into one column list, and then matched conflict targets against a suffix of that merged list. It was also matching the words ON CONFLICT inside the query file's own explanatory comment, which quotes the very statement it explains. Fixed by reading one row per index through pg_index.indkey with indnkeyatts, matching row per index through pg_index.indkey with indnkeyatts, matching on an order-insensitive column set after empirically confirming PostgreSQL accepts either order, and stripping SQL comments before scanning while preserving string literals. Mutation-tested afterwards: the reintroduced defect is caught and named. (4) The harness was flaky in a way that reported a migration failure rather than a harness failure: pg_isready succeeds while PostgreSQL is still in startup recovery, and _read_version ignored the return code of its own query, so the first sweep after a cold Docker cache failed db-0002 with FATAL: the database system is starting up. Readiness now requires a statement to succeed as well as pg_isready, and _read_version raises instead of reporting 'unknown version'. The database gates were re-run to confirm. Two further errors were made and repaired during the work rather than shipped: a PowerShell append that risked writing a UTF-8 BOM into a migration file, and a first version of the down-body script that omitted the marker and so wrote DROP statements into the up body. Both are now guarded in the scripts themselves, so the mistake cannot recur silently.

claim: All three of WI-108's acceptance criteria hold against a running PostgreSQL 17, not merely on inspection. The compose stack comes up healthy, refuses to start when any credential is unset, and the whole migration set applies into the dev database as the application role rather than as the bootstrap superuser. The dev role is refused by the test database and the test role is refused by the dev database, both by permission denial rather than by a failed connection, and no database named paper, shadow, or live exists at all. No credential is written down anywhere in the repository: every secret in the compose file is a required environment reference, .env is git-ignored and untracked, and .env.example declares each secret with an empty value.
method: Wrote infra/compose.yaml, a single pinned postgres:17-alpine service published on loopback only, with all three secrets expressed as ${VAR:?message} so the stack refuses to start rather than falling back to a default. Wrote infra/postgres/init/10-environments.sh, which creates one NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE role and one owned database per local environment, revokes CONNECT from PUBLIC before granting it to the owning role alone, and then proves the isolation by attempting both cross-environment connections and aborting initialisation if either succeeds. Wrote scripts/verify_local_env.py, which brings the stack up, replays every migration up body as the application role over TCP, and asserts the isolation in both directions. Because the no-credential criterion is a property of the committed tree rather than of a running container, it is asserted statically in tests/ci/test_local_env.py, which runs without Docker. The mutation set is: credential given a default password, isolation revoke removed, application role made superuser, loopback binding widened to all interfaces, paper environment provisioned locally, isolation failure no longer aborting initialisation, isolation probe result no longer gating the abort, init directory mounted writable, postgres image unpinned, init script converted to CRLF, and the LF rule dropped from .gitattributes.
